newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Asia debt appeals to U.S. mainstream.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Asia debt appeals to U.S. mainstream.

text.p: The virtue of Asian fixed income securities as steady, undramatic growth assets will get its due recognition from more mainstream U.S. investors in 1997, said U.S. analysts and fund managers.

Asian debt markets largely escaped the "irrational exuberance" that Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan recently lamented, because it had a less compelling story to tell than the resurgent countries of Latin America and Eastern Europe, they said.
As U.S. investors cast nervous glances at global markets and wonder where to reinvest the profits of 1996, Asian debt should look attractive, experts said.
"Unlike some boom-and-bust emerging markets, Asian markets are steady, with few hiccups along the way," said Feroz Talyarkhan, associate director at Bear Stearns and Co.
Talyarkhan said he expected the credit quality of Asian debt issuers to improve as the the export-driven economies in the region pull out of their 1997 slump.

Ismail Dalla, president of Washington Asset Management Inc, said a portfolio of carefully-selected Asian debt could generate 400 to 500 basis points over the yield of two-year U.S. Treasury notes next year.
In 1996, the Asian funds under his management had a 14 percent return in dollar terms.
Unlike the rollercoaster rides in equity investment, Asian fixed income assets appreciate over time on strong regional and country-specific fundamentals, Dalla said.
High rates of savings and investment and increasing intra-regional trade are the bedrock for a sustained high growth rate in that part of the world, he said.

Closely linked to the U.S. dollar, Asian currencies give dollar-based investors less currency risk, Dalla said, noting that even the Thai baht, which came under speculative attack this year, had a volatility of only plus or minus 1/2 percent.

The dollar's strength in 1996 has hurt the export performance of Asian tigers, but even if the dollar remains strong next year, those countries are in a better position to compete in the global marketplace, said Suhas Ketkar, a managing director at CS First Boston.
Countries like South Korea have adjusted to the stronger dollar by boosting productivity and competitiveness, much as Japan did when the yen appreciated earlier in the decade, he said.
Without big splashes, mainstream U.S. investors have been adding Asian debt to their portfolios, said Warren Allderidge, a managing director of Peregrine Investments.
He estimated they collectively hold $10 billion in Yankee bonds, 144A issues and bank loans, and the volume is likely to rise as more Asian paper is floated in the coming years.
John Praveen, senior international economist at Merrill Lynch, agreed that supply is increasing as Asian corporations shift from equities to debt capital.
"Debt is less expensive," he said, adding that as a less volatile asset than equities, debt attracts a larger pool of global institutional investors.

Reflecting the trend, major Asian markets have made large strides in developing debt market infrastructure, and the proliferation of local rating agencies have made credit risk more transparent, said Dalla of Washington Asset Management.
In India alone, five local agencies are checking public and private sector debts. Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia also have their native-grown agencies, he noted.
Among Asian debt issuers, Korea remains number one in volume, followed by India and Singapore, Dalla said.

The Philippines exemplified the new type of issuers on raising its international profile, he said. After receiving a BB rating from Standard and Poor's and Ba2 from Moody's, it launched a successful global bond to retire some Brady bonds.
On Hong Kong's imminent return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, U.S. analysts said they expected a smooth transition, with no noticeable effect on the regional market.

Preoccupied with domestic tasks of equalizing income between rich and poor provinces and the continuing reform of state enterprises, China is unlikely to meddle with Hong Kong's capitalist system, Peregrine's Allderidge said.
But Washington Asset Management's Dalla said he doubted China would completely leave Hong Kong alone to run its monetary affairs.
"Equity investors may have less to fear," he said. "but I would underweight Hong Kong debt."
